bib.title: Processing Raw Text (Chapter 3, Natural Language Processing with Python)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly, NLTK book); year not printed in the chapter text

question: How do we get raw text from the Web and disk, split it into words and sentences, normalise it (stemming, lemmatisation) and format output, using Python strings, Unicode and regular expressions?
contributions: Pipeline from URL/file to raw string to tokens to nltk.Text to normalised vocabulary (Fig 3-1)
Regex toolkit for word patterns, stems and tokenisation
Segmentation as search with an objective and simulated annealing

limits: Python 2 throughout: print statements, from urllib import urlopen, raw_input, 'rU' mode, u'' literals, str vs unicode, integer division needing from __future__ import division, wc = width/4 in Example 3-1.
nltk.clean_html() was removed from NLTK (raises NotImplementedError in 3.x); the book itself points to Beautiful Soup. The sample also shows a typo nltk.html_clean.

nltk.word_tokenize, the Punkt pickle path 'tokenizers/punkt/english.pickle' and nltk.data.find usage have changed; Punkt now loads via nltk.sent_tokenize and needs a data download. WordNet and corpora need nltk.download.
Regex quantifier {,n} (e.g. [a-z]{,6}) is used in Table 3-3 and examples; in Python 3 re it is valid but check behaviour per version.
Table 3-2 lists s.titlecase(), which is not a real str method (the method is title()).
Stemmer/lemmatizer outputs are on one 38-token sentence only: no accuracy or retrieval-effect measurement. Lemmatizer called without POS tags.
Segmentation is a toy (4 utterances, 55 characters), single stochastic run, no seed; annealing outputs vary. Google counts (2005) are inconsistent over time and region as the authors note.
Unicode coverage predates Python 3, where str is Unicode and encoding handled by open(..., encoding=).
No treatment of subword tokenisation (BPE, WordPiece), which is what modern LLM pipelines use.
practices: Use NLTK's off-the-shelf stemmers rather than a hand-written regex stemmer, since they handle irregular cases (3.6).
Pick Porter for indexing/search over word variants; pick the WordNet lemmatizer when you need a vocabulary of valid lemmas (3.6).
Prefix every regex string with r'...' so backslashes reach the re library (3.4).
Use non-greedy *? when splitting a stem from a suffix, and (?:...) when parentheses only group (3.5).
Splitting on whitespace is inadequate; tokenise with a regex or nltk.word_tokenize, and decide what counts as a token by application domain (3.7).
Use nltk.regexp_tokenize with the (?x) verbose flag and comments for readability; evaluate a tokenizer against gold-standard tokens such as the Penn Treebank sample (3.7).
Handle contractions with a lookup table, e.g. didn't -> did + n't (3.7).
Segment text into sentences before word tokenising when only a character stream is available; use Punkt (3.8).
Map non-standard words (numbers, abbreviations) to special tokens to shrink the vocabulary (3.6).
Web text contains headers, footers and markup that must be stripped, often by manual inspection of boundary strings (3.1).
Decode files to Unicode on input and encode on output; the 'plain text' notion is a fiction (3.3).
Beware false positives and false negatives when pattern-searching a corpus (3.5).
Normalise case before counting characters or word types (3.2, 3.6).

code.snippet:
def stem(word):
    regexp = r'^(.*?)(ing|ly|ed|ious|ies|ive|es|s|ment)?$'
    stem, suffix = re.findall(regexp, word)[0]
    return stem

pattern = r'''(?x)    # set flag to allow verbose regexps
    ([A-Z]\.)+        # abbreviations, e.g. U.S.A.
  | \w+(-\w+)*        # words with optional internal hyphens
  | \$?\d+(\.\d+)?%?  # currency and percentages, e.g. $12.40, 82%
  | \.\.\.            # ellipsis
  | [][.,;"'?():-_`]  # these are separate tokens
'''
nltk.regexp_tokenize(text, pattern)

porter = nltk.PorterStemmer()
lancaster = nltk.LancasterStemmer()
wnl = nltk.WordNetLemmatizer()

def segment(text, segs):
    words = []
    last = 0
    for i in range(len(segs)):
        if segs[i] == '1':
            words.append(text[last:i+1])
            last = i+1
    words.append(text[last:])
    return words

def evaluate(text, segs):
    words = segment(text, segs)
    text_size = len(words)
    lexicon_size = len(' '.join(list(set(words))))
    return text_size + lexicon_size
